hints: A fair die is thrown until a 6 is obtained. The probability of rolling a 6 on any throw is $p = \frac{1}{6}$, so failure probability is $q = \frac{5}{6}$.
Taking more than 8 throws means the first 8 throws must all fail to produce a 6.
walkthrough:
Model the number of throws until the first 6 with a geometric distribution where $p = \dfrac{1}{6}$ and $q = \dfrac{5}{6}$:
$$\mathrm{P}(X > 8) = q^8 = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^8$$
teacher_walkthrough: An ordinary fair die is thrown repeatedly until a 6 is obtained.
Let $X$ denote the number of throws up to and including the first 6.

Step 1: Identify the probability of success and failure.
$$p = \mathrm{P}(\text{rolling a 6}) = \frac{1}{6}$$
$$q = 1 - p = \frac{5}{6}$$

Step 2: Express 'takes more than 8 throws'.
If obtaining a 6 takes more than 8 throws, the first 6 has not appeared in any of the first 8 throws.
That is, each of the first 8 throws must be a non-6:
$$\mathrm{P}(X > 8) = q^8 = \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^8$$

Step 3: Compute the value:
$$5^8 = 390625$$
$$6^8 = 1679616$$
$$\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^8 = \frac{390625}{1679616} \approx 0.232568... \approx 0.233$$
Rounding to 3 significant figures gives $0.233$.

hints: For a pair of fair dice, obtaining a pair of 6s has probability $p = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}$.
Let $X$ be the number of throws of the pair of dice until a pair of 6s is obtained: $X \sim \mathrm{Geo}\left(\frac{1}{36}\right)$.
The expected value of a geometric random variable is given by $\mathrm{E}(X) = \frac{1}{p}$.
walkthrough:
Identify the parameter $p$ for obtaining a pair of 6s:
$$p = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{36}$$

Apply the formula for the expectation of a geometric distribution:
$$\mathrm{E}(X) = \dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{1}{1/36} = 36$$
teacher_walkthrough: Two fair dice are thrown repeatedly until a pair of 6s is obtained.
Let $X$ be the number of throws until a pair of 6s is rolled.

Step 1: Determine the probability of success $p$ on each trial.
Since each die is fair and independent:
$$p = \mathrm{P}(\text{first die is 6}) \times \mathrm{P}(\text{second die is 6}) = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}$$

Step 2: Identify the distribution.
$X$ follows a geometric distribution with parameter $p = \frac{1}{36}$:
$$X \sim \mathrm{Geo}\left(\frac{1}{36}\right)$$

Step 3: Calculate the expected value using $\mathrm{E}(X) = \frac{1}{p}$:
$$\mathrm{E}(X) = \frac{1}{1/36} = 36$$
On average, it takes 36 throws to obtain a pair of 6s.

hints: We need the probability that $X$ is either 10 or 11: $\mathrm{P}(X = 10) + \mathrm{P}(X = 11)$.
Use the geometric probability mass function $\mathrm{P}(X = x) = q^{x-1} p$ where $p = \frac{1}{36}$ and $q = \frac{35}{36}$.
Write $\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\frac{1}{36}\right) + \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^{10} \left(\frac{1}{36}\right)$ and evaluate to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Express the required probability as the sum of two mutually exclusive geometric outcomes:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10 \text{ or } X = 11) = \mathrm{P}(X = 10) + \mathrm{P}(X = 11)$$

Substitute $p = \dfrac{1}{36}$ and $q = \dfrac{35}{36}$ into the geometric probability formula $\mathrm{P}(X = x) = q^{x-1} p$:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10) = \left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)$$
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 11) = \left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^{10} \left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)$$

Sum the two terms and compute the value:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10) \approx 0.021575, \quad \mathrm{P}(X = 11) \approx 0.020975$$
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10 \text{ or } 11) = 0.021575 + 0.020975 = 0.04255 \approx 0.0425$$
teacher_walkthrough: We want to find the probability that obtaining a pair of 6s takes either 10 or 11 throws.

Step 1: Set up the sum of probabilities.
Since the events $X = 10$ and $X = 11$ are mutually exclusive:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10 \text{ or } 11) = \mathrm{P}(X = 10) + \mathrm{P}(X = 11)$$

Step 2: Recall the probability mass function of a geometric distribution:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = x) = q^{x-1} p$$
where $p = \frac{1}{36}$ and $q = 1 - \frac{1}{36} = \frac{35}{36}$.

Step 3: Evaluate each probability:
For $x = 10$:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10) = \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\frac{1}{36}\right) \approx (0.77669) \times (0.027778) \approx 0.021575$$
For $x = 11$:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 11) = \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^{10} \left(\frac{1}{36}\right) \approx (0.75511) \times (0.027778) \approx 0.020975$$

Step 4: Factor and sum:
Alternatively, factor out $\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\frac{1}{36}\right)$:
$$\mathrm{P}(X = 10) + \mathrm{P}(X = 11) = \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\frac{1}{36}\right) \left(1 + \frac{35}{36}\right) = \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^9 \left(\frac{1}{36}\right) \left(\frac{71}{36}\right)$$
$$= 0.0215747 \times 1.972222 \approx 0.042550... \approx 0.0425$$
Rounding to 3 significant figures gives $0.0425$.
